strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting problem: moving beyond black-box EEG classifiers toward a Bayesian neural dynamical system that jointly infers latent event processes and a directed event-relational graph, motivated by electrophysiology (dLIF prior, STDP-shaped coupling).

The model composition (EPDE -> MELP -> ERG) is carefully motivated, and the authors are commendably honest that the dLIF prior is phenomenological on population-level rate dynamics rather than a claim about single-neuron dynamics (Sec. 1 and Sec. 4.3).

Rigorous cross-subject five-fold protocol with subject-level aggregation on two real AD EEG cohorts (Miltiadous et al. 2024; Sadegh-Zadeh et al. 2023), plus ablations of the dLIF and ERG priors (Table 3) that show each component contributes.

Appendices provide substantial implementation detail (architectures, shape tables, pseudocode, FLOPs/parameter counts in Table 4, additional sensitivity/specificity/AUC tables), and the impact statement is thoughtful about clinical misuse, dataset shift, and privacy.
weaknesses: The empirical case for the headline claim of 'superior performance over strong baselines' is contradicted by the authors' own supplementary results: on AD cohort B, LERD's AUC (0.8383) is substantially worse than ADFormer (0.9714) and most baselines (Table 6), and sensitivity/specificity advantages are mixed. The main text never reconciles this. Gains on cohort A are small relative to reported standard deviations, and no statistical significance tests are reported.

The toy benchmark is unconvincing. Baselines (NODE, ODE-RNN) report median rates of exactly 1.000 with degenerate [1.000,1.000] confidence intervals and uniformly zero IoU, which suggests the baselines were either misconfigured or are structurally incapable of event inference; comparing event-recovery of non-event-based neural ODEs is a weak strawman. The synthetic data (y = sin(t) + noise, exponential inter-event times) is far simpler than multichannel EEG, and LERD's 95% rate intervals are very wide (e.g., [10.5, 35.2] for a 17.5 Hz band), undercutting the uncertainty-calibration claim.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 contains a questionable step: the inequality 'integral over [0, -ε) <= |G(-2ε) - G(-ε)|' is not justified in general (the tail mass on [-ε, 0) need not be bounded by the mass on [-2ε, -ε]), and the appeal to Lemma B.1 to 'control the tail near the singular endpoint' is asserted rather than derived. The tightness of the bound for the fixed small ε used in training is never assessed empirically.

The 'stability guarantees' (Theorem A.1, Corollary A.2) are essentially the observation that exp(-α|x|) is α-Lipschitz plus triangle inequalities and standard sub-Gaussian concentration. Presenting these as a theoretical contribution substantially overstates their depth.

The variational formulation is muddled: the decoder conditions on X itself, so p(Y | X, T, G) leaves unclear what the latent variables are actually explaining; the objective mixes KL terms with ad hoc regularizers (Fisher-z matching, L2 rate consistency) whose weights are described only as 'modest default weights,' hurting reproducibility, and no code release is mentioned.

The ERG is regularized toward Pearson correlations via Fisher-z matching, so the later visualization (Fig. 3) showing ERG graphs resembling Pearson connectivity is partly by construction. The paper acknowledges this, but it weakens the claim that the graph provides independent timing-derived connectivity insight; no quantitative graph-recovery evaluation against a ground-truth interaction structure is provided (the toy data has no cross-channel coupling).

Cohort B contains only 7 MCI subjects, making macro-F1 and any multi-class conclusion fragile; class imbalance handling is not discussed. Known dynamical baselines from the related-work section (EEG microstates, HMM models, STRODE on the real cohorts) are absent from the real-data comparison.

The clinical neuroscience claims (Fig. 2 frequency slowing, Fig. 3 sparser connectivity in AD/FTD) rest on model-derived quantities with no ground truth; group-level mean differences are shown without inferential statistics, so 'physiology-aligned latent summaries' remains suggestive rather than validated.

strengths: The high-level goal is worthwhile and well-motivated: moving beyond black-box EEG classifiers toward latent event-level dynamics with a directed interaction graph, grounded in established EEG phenomenology (oscillatory slowing, connectivity disruption) and the STDP principle.
The paper is honest that the dLIF prior is phenomenological (population-level regularization rather than a single-neuron claim), which avoids overclaiming biological plausibility.

A reasonable cross-subject 5-fold evaluation protocol is used (subject-level splits, stratification, subject-level aggregation), and public datasets (Miltiadous et al. 2024; Sadegh-Zadeh et al. 2023) support reproducibility of the data side.
The impact statement appropriately discusses misuse as a standalone diagnostic, dataset shift, and privacy risks of EEG data.
Ablations (Table 3) show each prior component contributes, and the appendix provides pseudocode and shape summaries that partially support reimplementation.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of consistent superiority is contradicted by the paper's own tables. On cohort B, LERD has the LOWEST AUC of all methods (0.8383 vs. 0.9714 for ADFormer; Table 6), while claiming the best accuracy (89.82%). This discrepancy strongly suggests the accuracy gain is driven by class imbalance/threshold effects rather than better ranking, and the 'consistently outperforms strong baselines' claim in the abstract and Section 5.2 is not supported. LERD's macro-F1 on cohort B (64.87) is also not clearly better than baselines (ADFormer 63.89) and is below its own ERG-prior-only ablation (65.63).

No statistical significance testing is reported anywhere. Differences in Tables 2 and 3 are within reported standard deviations in many cases (e.g., cohort A: 75.03 ± 8.29 vs. 72.68 ± 4.57), so the claimed improvements cannot be distinguished from noise with 5 folds and small cohorts (7 MCI subjects in cohort B).

The synthetic evaluation appears misconfigured or unfair. Baselines report Median Rate 1.000 with CI [1.000, 1.000] and IoU exactly 0 across all bands, suggesting they were not given a meaningful way to express event structure rather than a genuine failure of 'purely data-driven' methods. The 'classification score (CS)' metric is never defined for what is a regression-style toy task (recovering event times of a sine process), making Table 1 hard to interpret.

Figure 4's visual comparison is misleading: STRODE panels use x-axes spanning 0–0.05 while LERD panels span 0–1, so the 'tighter diagonal alignment' is not a like-for-like comparison; the [10–15] and [15–20] LERD panels look essentially identical, raising concerns about figure quality or duplicated results.

The theoretical contributions are weak relative to the claims. Theorem A.1 is simply the observation that exp(−α|x|) is α-Lipschitz plus triangle inequalities—far short of a meaningful 'stability guarantee' contribution. Theorem 4.1's proof (Appendix B) invokes Lemma B.1 in a hand-wavy way and asserts a tail inequality (∫ over [−ε,0) ≤ |∫ over [−ε,−2ε]|) whose validity is not established; additionally, the bound U_ε evaluates G(−2ε) even though G is only defined on [−e^{−S}, −1), which is out of domain for ε near e^{−S}. The variational objective is a patchwork of surrogates (rate proxies, IVP–KL bound, weak Fisher–z regularizer), so calling the result a principled Bayesian/ELBO framework overstates its rigor.

The 'physiology-aligned latent summaries' do not clearly add value beyond standard spectral analysis. Figure 2's AD < MCI < HC frequency ordering replicates well-known EEG slowing that any PSD analysis would show; no quantitative comparison against conventional band-power or PSD baselines is provided to demonstrate the latent variable viewpoint adds insight. Similarly, similarity of ERG graphs to Pearson graphs is partly by construction, since the training objective includes a Fisher–z alignment term toward Pearson correlations (Eq. 25), which the authors themselves acknowledge—undermining the claim that the ERG is an independent, timing-derived connectivity summary.

Heavy naming (EPDE, MELP, dLIF, ERG) obscures that the components are relatively simple: an MLP predicting next-event times, a reparameterized lognormal mixture, an exponential kernel on event lags, and an L2 rate penalty. The framing as a novel 'Bayesian neural dynamical system' inflates the apparent novelty.

It is unclear whether gains come from the proposed priors or from the added GCN/fusion architecture: the 'no prior' ablation (70.52 on cohort A) exactly matches the LSTM baseline, and no ablation isolates the GCN graph branch alone with a generic adjacency.

Reproducibility gaps: no code release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters (loss weights λ_aux, λ_spk, λ_graph, λ_LIF, β, λ_LIF, ε, K, solver settings) are described only as 'modest default weights' without values, despite the objective being a sensitive combination of many terms.

Several presentational issues further reduce confidence: the IoU metric for graph/event recovery is undefined operationally; Table 1's CI interpretation is unclear; and claims like 'rigorously assessed' and 'superior performance' are repeated without matching evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting problem: moving beyond black-box EEG classifiers toward models that expose latent event dynamics and event-level interaction structure, which is a meaningful gap relative to the supervised AD-EEG literature reviewed in Section 2.

The overall system design (EPDE + MELP + dLIF prior + STDP-shaped ERG) is creative and clearly motivated, and the authors are commendably careful in places, e.g., explicitly framing the dLIF prior as phenomenological/population-level rather than claiming single-neuron interpretability (Section 1), and acknowledging that ERG–Pearson similarity is partly expected due to the Fisher–z alignment term (Section 6.2).

The evaluation includes a synthetic dataset with ground-truth event structure (Appendix E.2.1), two public AD EEG cohorts with a strict cross-subject five-fold protocol, ablations of both priors (Table 3), computational cost reporting (Table 4), and additional sensitivity/specificity/AUC tables (Tables 5–6), which is more complete than many comparable submissions.

The physiological summary in Figure 2 (central frequency decreasing with disease severity across AD < MCI < HC) is consistent with well-established EEG slowing findings, and the impact statement thoughtfully discusses misuse as a standalone diagnostic tool, dataset shift, and privacy risks.
Appendices include proofs for all theoretical claims and pseudocode/architecture tables that aid reimplementation.
weaknesses: The central claim that LERD 'consistently outperforms strong baselines' is contradicted by the paper's own evidence: in Table 5, LERD's AUC on cohort A (0.8143) is below LCADNet (0.8462), and in Table 6, LERD's AUC on cohort B (0.8383) is by far the worst of all seven methods (baselines 0.9486–0.9714), despite LERD having the best accuracy. This pattern (high accuracy, low AUC on a heavily imbalanced cohort with only 7 MCI subjects out of 168) suggests accuracy gains may be driven by class imbalance and threshold placement rather than genuinely better ranking of diseased subjects. No statistical significance tests are reported for any comparison.

The synthetic evaluation is not convincing. The 'CS' (classification score) metric in Table 1 is never precisely defined for an unlabeled toy dataset, and the headline IoU numbers (0.473/0.289/0.202) are single values with no repeats, error bars, or significance tests. The baselines chosen (NODE, ODE-RNN, STRODE) are not event-process recovery methods, so zero IoU is unsurprising and the comparison feels somewhat strawman-like. Moreover, the claimed rate recovery is weak: on the [5–10] Hz band with true rates near 7.5, LERD's median is 7.532 but the 95% CI is [4.300, 14.867], and STRODE's is [0.269, 0.410]; the text's claim that uncertainty intervals 'align closely with the true frequency band intervals' overstates results where the CI spans more than the entire target band.

There is a circularity concern in the interpretability claims: the dLIF prior encodes a 'plausible alpha/theta-to-beta frequency range' (Appendix F.3) and the ERG is aligned to observable Pearson correlations via the Fisher–z regularizer. The headline physiological findings (band slowing consistent with the prior's imposed range; connectivity resembling correlation graphs the model is nudged toward) may partly reflect priors the authors injected rather than structure discovered from data. The paper does not disentangle what the model learned from what was imposed.

The theoretical contributions are thin relative to how they are framed. Theorem 4.1's 'IVP-based upper bound' amounts to numerically evaluating the KL integral via an ODE with a tail correction near the singular endpoint; it is a computable evaluation scheme rather than a substantive relaxation of the intractable path KL, and the paper does not quantify how loose Uε is in practice. Lemma B.1 is imported from prior work (Huang et al., 2021). Theorem A.1 and Corollary A.2 are straightforward consequences of Lipschitz composition and the triangle inequality.

There is an internal inconsistency about the ERG's structure: the contributions and related work emphasize recovering a 'directed, event-level interaction graph', yet the implementation symmetrizes the adjacency for the GCN (Section 4.6 'optionally symmetrize', and Appendix F.4 states 'a symmetric adjacency'), and the theory in Appendix A treats the perturbed adjacency entry-wise without addressing directionality. The practical model does not clearly deliver the directed-interaction capability that motivates the work.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data-split release is mentioned; the loss weights are described only as 'modest default weights and found them robust across cohorts' without values; the KL_T surrogate construction (Eq. 8's g(m)) is dense and would be hard to reimplement exactly; and the toy 'CS' metric cannot be reproduced from the manuscript.

Multiple strong claims in the abstract and Sections 5–6 ('rigorously assessed', 'superior accuracy and robustness', 'consistently outperforms') are not supported at the level of rigor claimed, given single-run or unpaired results, wide variances (e.g., LERD 75.03 ± 8.29 vs. LEAD 72.68 ± 4.57), and the contradictory AUC results. Presentation is generally readable but the gap between narrative and evidence is a recurring problem.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely interesting and well-motivated problem: annotation-free recovery of latent event timing and cross-channel relational structure from multichannel EEG, going beyond black-box label prediction. The framing is clearly articulated, and the authors are commendably careful about interpretation (e.g., the ERG is explicitly positioned as a sensor-level, timing-derived summary rather than causal effective connectivity, and the dLIF prior is framed as phenomenological).

The model is an ambitious, coherent unification of several components (EPDE event posterior, lognormal mixture inter-event sampling, dLIF physiological prior, STDP-shaped event-relational graph) under one variational objective, with a clean end-to-end training recipe.

Experimental hygiene is above average for this area: a five-fold cross-subject protocol with subject-level stratification and majority-vote aggregation, structural-recovery metrics (IoU) on synthetic data with known generative structure, prior ablations (Table 4), one-factor sensitivity sweeps (Table 8), computational cost reporting (Table 5), and extended metrics (Tables 6-7).

The empirical AD-slowing trend in Figure 2 / Table 9 (inferred central frequency ordered HC > MCI > AD across 18-19 channels) is a nice model-derived summary consistent with established neurophysiology, and the paper does not overclaim source-level causality.

The impact statement thoughtfully discusses risks (standalone diagnostic misuse, dataset shift, privacy) and mitigations, and limitations such as volume conduction and mixing confounds are acknowledged in the introduction rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The headline claim that LERD 'consistently outperforms strong baselines' is not fully supported by the reported metrics. On both cohorts, LERD's AUC is inferior to baselines (Cohort A: 0.8143 vs. LCADNet's 0.8462; Cohort B: 0.8383 vs. ADFormer's 0.9714, the lowest in Table 7) even though LERD has the highest accuracy. This accuracy-vs-AUC inconsistency, which could arise from thresholding or majority-vote aggregation effects, is never analyzed or explained. The paper cites sensitivity/specificity/AUC as supporting evidence but these actually undercut the superiority claim.

There are no statistical significance tests anywhere. Reported gains (e.g., 75.03±8.29 vs. 72.68±4.57 on Cohort A; 89.82±8.39 vs. 82.38±14.71 on Cohort B) come with large overlapping standard deviations across only five folds, on small cohorts (Cohort B has only 7 MCI subjects). Differences of a few points under this variance are not clearly distinguishable from noise, and no corrections for multiple comparisons are provided.

The theoretical contributions are weaker than advertised. Theorem 4.1 is essentially a change-of-variables identity for a KL integral, and the 'stability guarantees' for the ERG (Theorem A.2, Corollary A.3) reduce to the global Lipschitzness of exp(-alpha|x|) composed with averaging and Gaussian concentration - standard results with little model-specific content. Lemma A.1 is imported directly from Huang et al. (2021). The theory adds polish rather than substantive new understanding.

The sensitivity sweep in Table 8 undermines the claim of robustness to auxiliary weights: accuracy fluctuates over roughly an 8-point range (e.g., ERG weight 10^-4 gives 63.73% vs. 10^-8 giving 75.03%), which contradicts the text that performance 'degrades mainly when weights become poorly scaled.' The optimal IVP-KL weight (5x10^-10) is strikingly small, raising questions about how much of the objective is actually active during training.

The synthetic benchmark is very limited (20 observations per sequence from a single sinusoid plus Gaussian noise), and the toy result that all baselines obtain IoU exactly 0.000 while LERD obtains 0.2-0.47 suggests a possibly degenerate comparison; no statistical uncertainty is attached to the IoU values, and how IoU is computed on continuous posterior event-time distributions is not described in enough detail.

Key methodological details are underspecified relative to the paper's ambition. The evidence linking inferred events to real electrophysiological phenomena rests largely on qualitative inspection of density plots (Figure 2) and graph visualizations (Figure 3) without quantitative statistical validation (e.g., group-level tests on inferred frequencies or graph statistics). The claimed code release has an empty URL ('Our code is available at:'), harming reproducibility. Some references are dated 2026 and cite venues (ICLR 2026, ICML 2026) that raise citation-integrity questions.

Baseline fairness is uncertain: the paper benchmarks against several strong supervised models but argues that point-process/GLM approaches are not drop-in baselines, leaving the closest competing annotation-free method (STRODE) evaluated mainly on synthetic data. The ERG regularizer anchors the learned graph to Pearson correlations, and while ablations (no-prior / dLIF-only / ERG-only) are provided, it remains unclear how much of the downstream gain comes from the added graph features versus the interpretable event machinery itself.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely interesting and underexplored problem: annotation-free recovery of latent event timing and cross-channel relational structure from multichannel EEG, rather than pure label prediction. The framing in Section 2 (contrasting with DCM, HMM/microstate, and point-process GLM approaches, and honestly explaining why classical point-process models are not drop-in baselines when events are latent) is fair and well-positioned.

The system design is thoughtful and end-to-end: the EPDE posterior over next-event times, the lognormal-mixture MELP with reparameterized sampling, and the electrophysiology-inspired dLIF prior (with refractory gating and a population-level, explicitly non-single-neuron interpretation carefully stated) form a coherent pipeline.

Ablations (Table 4) separate the contributions of the dLIF prior, the ERG prior, and the dual-prior configuration, and the no-prior variant is reported, which supports the claim that gains are not obtained merely by anchoring the graph to Pearson correlations.

The subject-level five-fold cross-subject protocol, computational cost reporting (Table 5), auxiliary-weight sensitivity sweeps (Table 8), and the honest discussion of high variance in imbalanced Cohort B are good reproducibility and evaluation practices.

The impact statement is substantive, addressing misuse as a standalone diagnostic tool, dataset shift, and EEG privacy, and the model-derived frequency summaries (Figure 2, Table 9) align with known AD slowing in an easily checkable way.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is overclaimed. Theorem 4.1 is a routine change of variables: the 'IVP representation' of the KL is just the KL integral written in terms of an antiderivative G evaluated at the endpoint (Eq. 9-10). The ERG 'stability guarantees' (Theorem A.2, Corollary A.3) are elementary Lipschitz bounds on exp(-alpha|x|) plus textbook Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions; Lemma A.1 is imported from Huang et al. (2021). These results are correct but do not constitute a substantive theory contribution.

A serious empirical inconsistency undermines the central claim that LERD 'consistently outperforms strong baselines': on AD cohort B, LERD has the LOWEST AUC of all methods (0.8383 vs. 0.9486-0.9714 for baselines, Table 7), and on cohort A, LCADNet's AUC (0.8462) also exceeds LERD's (0.8143, Table 6). The accuracy advantage (89.82% on cohort B) combined with the worst AUC suggests the headline gain comes from majority-vote/threshold aggregation effects rather than better ranking quality, yet the paper never discusses or explains this contradiction.

The toy benchmark results are not convincing evidence of latent-structure recovery. In Table 1, NODE and ODE-RNN report a median rate of exactly 1.000 with degenerate confidence intervals [1.000, 1.000], which strongly suggests the baselines either do not output rates at all or the metric is not applicable to them, making the comparison ill-posed. Additionally, the appendix defines 'CS' as a classification score on a toy dataset that (from the generation description yi = sin(ti) + noise) appears to contain no class labels, while Table 1 uses cosine similarity - the evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent.

There is a discrepancy between the claimed directed event-lag graph and the implementation: the main text repeatedly emphasizes a 'directed' event-relational graph built from cross-channel event lags (Section 4.1, 4.6), but Algorithm 3 computes symmetric weights Wij = exp(-gamma|si - sj|) from time-averaged trajectory values (not event lags) and explicitly enforces symmetry (W = (W + W^T)/2); Appendix F.4 likewise describes a symmetric adjacency. The actual mechanism appears to differ from the paper's central narrative.

The improvements on the real AD datasets are modest relative to the reported standard deviations (e.g., 75.03 +/- 8.29 vs. 72.68 +/- 4.57 for LEAD on cohort A; cohort B differences overlap heavily), and the sensitivity sweeps in Table 8 show differences (e.g., 71.63 at IVP-KL weight 0 vs. 75.03 at 5e-10) that are small compared to the fold-to-fold variance, weakening claims that the auxiliary machinery is decisively responsible for the gains.

There is an identification concern: all training signal on real data is the label cross-entropy (Algorithm 4, line 14), while Y is stated not to supervise the latent events or relations. Nothing in the presented evidence rules out that the EPDE/MELP 'events' are largely an arbitrary re-encoding of encoder features shaped by the priors, rather than recovered latent event structure - particularly given that the ERG regularizer (Eq. 21) is anchored to Pearson correlations computed from X, blurring the line between learned timing structure and trivially available signal statistics.

Reproducibility is undermined by the empty code link (footnote 1 reads 'Our code is available at:' with no URL), and several methodological details (e.g., the exact relation between the STDP-shaped edge map in Section 4.1 and the trajectory-distance kernel in Algorithm 3, the definition of the toy 'CS' metric) cannot be resolved from the manuscript.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely under-explored problem: annotation-free joint recovery of latent event timing and event-lag interaction structure from multichannel EEG, rather than pure label prediction. The framing as a Bayesian latent event-relational dynamical system is coherent and well-motivated.

The variational objective (Eq. 1) is thoughtfully decomposed, and the paper is unusually transparent about approximations: the path-measure KL is replaced by a tractable IVP-based rate surrogate, and the ERG regularizer is described as a weak observable anchoring rather than supervision. Ablations (Table 4) and weight-sensitivity sweeps (Table 8, E.5) directly probe whether gains come from forcing the graph to match correlations.

Evaluation hygiene is above average for this domain: a five-fold cross-subject protocol, subject-level majority-vote aggregation, per-window FLOPs/params/runtime comparisons (Tables 3, 5), supplementary sensitivity/specificity/AUC tables, and an honest impact statement discussing misuse as a standalone diagnostic tool, dataset shift, and EEG privacy.

The synthetic benchmark provides ground-truth event structure, enabling structural recovery metrics (IoU) rather than only downstream accuracy; the paper also explains why point-process GLM baselines are not drop-in competitors in this latent-event regime (Section 2.2), which is a fair and careful positioning.

The physiological validation (Figure 2, Table 9: inferred central frequency ordering HC > MCI > AD across 18/19 channels) is consistent with well-established AD EEG slowing, giving qualitative external validity to the latent summaries.
weaknesses: A central architectural claim is contradicted by the implementation. The paper repeatedly advertises a 'directed event-relational graph' with an 'STDP-shaped mapping' encoding how events in one channel 'precede, follow, or align' with others (Sections 1, 4.1, contributions). However, the edge map is exp(-alpha|Delta t|) (Eq. 22 area), which is symmetric in the sign of the lag and therefore cannot distinguish precedence direction; moreover, Algorithm 3 explicitly symmetrizes the adjacency (W <- 1/2(W + W^T)) and Appendix F.4 describes 'a symmetric adjacency.' The directedness claim, and the STDP analogy, are not supported by what is actually computed.

The main-text claim that LERD 'consistently outperforms strong baselines' is undermined by the appendix AUC results the paper does not discuss: on Cohort B, LERD's AUC (0.8383 ± 0.0578, Table 7) is clearly the worst among compared models, versus ADFormer at 0.9714; on Cohort A, LCADNet has the best AUC (0.8462 vs LERD 0.8143). Since LERD is presented as providing calibrated latent probabilities, this contradiction between accuracy/F1 and AUC deserves analysis rather than silence. No statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, and several accuracy gaps (e.g., 75.03 ± 8.29 vs 72.68 ± 4.57 on Cohort A) are within one standard deviation.

The theoretical contributions are modest relative to their billing. Theorem 4.1 is essentially a change of variables (m = -e^{-t}) plus an integrability argument; Theorem A.2 is a two-step Lipschitz composition, and Lemma A.1 is imported from prior work. The 'IVP representation' G'(m) = g(m) with g defined directly in terms of q and p is a formal repackaging rather than a new analytical tool. Additionally, the posterior in Eq. (16), q(t|x) = -(Phi)'(t)/t, is asserted to be a density without verifying non-negativity or integrability, and the link between the ideal IVP (Eqs. 12-14) and the neural surrogate f_theta_Phi (Eq. 15) is loose: the surrogate replaces the IVP solution outright, so the 'EPDE' is largely a name for a learned next-event-time update.

The toy experiment raises questions about what is being measured. NODE/ODE-RNN report 'Median Rate 1.000, 95% CI [1.000, 1.000]', which looks like a placeholder rather than a genuine rate estimate, making the rate comparison in Table 1 largely vacuous for those baselines. LERD's own absolute IoU (0.20-0.47) is modest, and its rate confidence intervals ([4.3, 14.9] for a band centered at 7.5) are wide. The terminology 'classification score (CS)' for cosine similarity on a synthetic dataset with no classification task is confusing.

Cohort B contains only 7 MCI subjects, and the paper itself attributes large baseline variance to this; combined with the reported fold-level swings and the AUC discrepancy, the clinical claims on Cohort B should be tempered. Fairness of comparison to LEAD (an EEG foundation model) is not discussed, e.g., whether its pretraining corpus could overlap the evaluation cohorts.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code availability footnote is empty ('Our code is available at:' with no URL). The method description spans many interacting components (encoder, EPDE surrogate, MELP, dLIF rate proxy, ERG, GCN, fusion) with 'modest default weights' only loosely specified, making independent reimplementation difficult; the sensitivity sweeps in Table 8 show accuracy varying by several points across orders of magnitude of each weight.

Group-level physiological conclusions (e.g., Figure 2, Figure 3) are supported qualitatively without statistical testing of between-group differences in inferred frequencies or graph densities, leaving the 'mechanistic insight' contribution suggestive rather than demonstrated.
